title: 🪨 Hera's First Images Reveal a Stadium-Sized Crater on Asteroid Dimorphos — and Hundreds of Rocks Orbiting It!
body: 🪨 Hera's First Images Reveal a Stadium-Sized Crater on Asteroid Dimorphos — and Hundreds of Rocks Orbiting It!

The European Space Agency has published today the first detailed images from its Hera spacecraft of the site where the DART spacecraft struck the small asteroid Dimorphos, revealing a huge crater the size of a sports field that completely flattened one face of the asteroid — the first close look at the results of the first planetary defense test in history.

The main image was taken from a distance of 29 kilometers on November 7 at a resolution of 2.7 meters per pixel, and shows the crater spanning almost the entire width of the asteroid's struck face, with a strange cigar-like structure at its center, while the rest of the rock remained almost unchanged — a surprise the mission's principal investigator summed up by saying that the answer to the question 'did a crater form, did the shape change, or did it stay the same?' turned out to be all three.

NASA's DART spacecraft had deliberately crashed into Dimorphos in September 2022 at a speed of about 22,000 kilometers per hour, shortening its orbit around the larger asteroid Didymos by 33 minutes — and now Hera has revealed a second surprise: hundreds of unknown rocks, some ranging in size from a football to a washing machine, orbiting the two asteroids, whose discovery three weeks ago was a difficult challenge for the team of the accompanying small satellites.

Dimorphos is about 151 meters in diameter, while Didymos is about 730 meters across, and the smaller one orbits the larger at a distance of about one kilometer — and Hera used three instruments in its first survey: a thermal infrared imager to measure surface temperature, a multispectral imager with 25 colors, and a monochrome camera.

The work is still just beginning: the spacecraft will approach to a distance of only 13 kilometers in December to capture clearer images and measure the mass of the two asteroids, then launch two small satellites in January 2027 to come even closer, and one of them may attempt to land on the surface of Dimorphos — and all these measurements will help in understanding how effective the impact was and improving strategies to deflect dangerous asteroids in the future.

Simply put: after four years of waiting, we have finally seen the crater left by the first deliberate collision with an asteroid, along with hundreds of rocks drifting around it — so does it reassure you that humanity is now testing how to stop an asteroid from hitting Earth?
If an asteroid approached Earth, do you trust that we could deflect it before it is too late?
